{"id":"persona-lnaj","title":"No general file-drop identity source; every file path is compiled in","description":"There is no general way to hand personad an identity from a file. Every file-based source today is a vendor path compiled into Rust: oidc.rs hardcodes ~/.config/gcloud/application_default_credentials.json and ~/.azure/*, and did_key.rs does not read a file at all, it reads the PERSONA_DID_KEYS environment variable. Adding a source means writing an attestor and shipping a release.

PROPOSAL. A drop directory, something like ~/.config/persona/identities/, that the daemon scans. Anything a user or a script can write there becomes visible to the daemon without persona knowing anything about where it came from.

THE ARCHITECTURE ALREADY SPLITS THIS CORRECTLY, which is why it is worth doing now rather than before this week. persona-okek separated enumerate(), which yields a Candidate carrying no assurance and no presence, from prove(), which yields Evidence. A dropped file falls cleanly on one side or the other:

  UNSIGNED FILE, e.g. a line saying alice@example.com
    Anyone who can write the user's home directory can write it, so it is
    self-assertion and not evidence. It should produce a Candidate and nothing
    more. prove() cannot succeed on it, so Claim::derive returns None and the
    daemon declines. That is not a shortcoming; it is the model working. The file
    names an identity the daemon can talk about, and some other attestor may be
    able to prove it.

  SIGNED CREDENTIAL, e.g. a JWT from an IdP, an X.509 certificate, a signed
  statement
    The daemon verifies the issuer signature and produces Evidence::IdpVerified,
    the same variant VerifiedToken already exists for. This is the case that can
    actually mint a credential.

WHY IT IS WORTH MORE THAN ANOTHER ATTESTOR. It is the escape hatch for every source persona does not natively support, and it converts a category of future Rust work into a shell script. A new vendor stops being an attestor to write and becomes a file to produce. oidc.rs's two hardcoded paths become instances of the general mechanism rather than special cases. It is also testable with no hardware, which matters for CI and for contributors who have no PIV card or FIDO2 key.

It is the natural landing place for two things already discussed: derived PIV credentials under SP 800-157, which are exactly a credential a file can carry; and a phone acting as a remote attestor, which has to hand the desktop something eventually.

WHAT MUST BE GOT RIGHT, and none of it is optional:

  Directory trust. The drop path must be owned by the user and not group- or
  world-writable, refused otherwise. persona-grpc/src/server.rs already does this
  check for the socket directory in prepare_socket_dir; reuse that reasoning
  rather than inventing a second one.

  No evidence without a verifiable signature. An unsigned file must never reach
  Evidence. The tier() match makes this hard to get wrong, but it must be stated.

  A trust anchor. Verifying a signed credential needs an issuer key from
  somewhere. That is the unsolved part, and it overlaps persona-5s4b.103, which
  says persona enroll reports authorization it never performs and no enrollment
  state exists anywhere. A drop directory without a way to say which issuers are
  trusted is a directory that accepts anything.

  Replay and freshness. A static signed file can be copied to another machine.
  Without an embedded expiry or a freshness bound it is a bearer token sitting on
  disk. persona-ogiv now carries an attestation timestamp through Claim::derive,
  so the material for a freshness rule exists, but a file-sourced credential must
  be dated by the credential rather than by when the daemon read the file.

  Format. One documented format, not a guessing parser. A guessing parser over
  attacker-influenceable files in a directory is a trust boundary the project
  rules say not to be lazy about.

SUGGESTED SEQUENCING: unsigned candidates first, because they need no trust anchor and exercise the directory-trust and format work; signed credentials once enrollment gives somewhere for issuer keys to live.","status":"open","priority":2,"issue_type":"feature","owner":"mark@reviewcommit.com","created_at":"2026-09-14T22:11:14.441387491Z","created_by":"agent","updated_at":"2026-09-14T22:11:14.441387491Z","labels":["attestors","design"]}

{"notes":"FORMAT DECISION, from the owner: a DID, or an extensible JSON credential format. Both, at different layers, and the split maps onto the Candidate/Evidence split exactly.

IDENTIFIER: a DID. This is already the spec's direction, not a new idea. SPEC-HIA:207-210 names did:key, did:ipfs and did:web with an assurance mapping, iaa1 for did:key as self-issued and iaa2 for did:web under a domain the user controls. SPEC-HIA:141 maps a personal.{user} trust domain to the user's DID document. did_key.rs already accepts did:key URIs, just from the PERSONA_DID_KEYS environment variable rather than a file, so a drop directory is a small generalisation of something that exists.

  A bare DID in a file is an IDENTIFIER, not a credential. It names an identity and
  proves nothing, so it produces a Candidate and stops there. That is the correct
  outcome and needs no trust anchor at all, which is why it should ship first.

CREDENTIAL: a signed JWT carrying a credential, not JSON-LD. W3C VC-DM is the obvious
citation and the wrong implementation here. Data Integrity proofs over JSON-LD require
canonicalisation and @context resolution, which is a large machine to add to a daemon
that currently parses one audience string with split(). VC-JWT, a JWT whose payload is
the credential, gets the same extensibility through ordinary JSON claims and verifies
with the JOSE stack already in the tree. persona already signs and verifies ES256 and
publishes a JWKS.

  SD-JWT VC is worth evaluating rather than assuming, and I am flagging it as a
  question rather than a recommendation because I am not current on its status: it is
  an IETF draft last I knew, and the EU Digital Identity Wallet is built on it. Two
  reasons it may fit better than plain VC-JWT. It is the format an EU wallet will
  actually hand out, which matters given the OpenHarmony and EU-foundation interest.
  And its selective disclosure is the same property persona already pursues with
  per-consumer pseudonyms, one layer up: a credential can carry many claims and
  disclose only the ones a particular consumer needs. Check the draft's status before
  committing to it.

THE NETWORK DECISION, which this forces and which is bigger than the format.

personad makes ZERO outbound network connections today. Verified: the only network
reference anywhere in the workspace is the ponytail note in did_key.rs saying "upgrade
path: reqwest + did-web resolver once networking is desired". For a local identity
daemon that is a property worth naming and probably worth keeping.

  did:key is self-contained. The public key IS the identifier, so verifying a
  credential issued by a did:key issuer requires no resolution, no network, no
  resolver cache, and no new failure mode. It preserves the zero-network property.

  did:web requires an HTTPS fetch of a DID document. That gives the daemon an
  outbound dependency, a cache with invalidation questions, behaviour that varies
  with the network, and a new attack surface reachable by whoever controls the
  domain in a dropped file.

So: did:key first, did:web only behind an explicit decision that the daemon may make
network calls. That decision deserves its own bead rather than arriving as a side
effect of a file format. did:ipfs is further still.

REVISED SEQUENCING:
  1. Drop directory accepting bare did:key identifiers -> Candidate. No trust anchor,
     no network, no signature verification. Generalises PERSONA_DID_KEYS and shakes
     out directory-trust and format handling.
  2. VC-JWT signed by a did:key issuer -> Evidence::IdpVerified. Verification is a
     JOSE operation against a key embedded in the issuer's own identifier. Still no
     network.
  3. did:web, only after the network-posture decision."}
